In many real-world scenarios, users interact with digital systems while their hands are partially occupied, such as when holding tools or everyday objects. Prior work on busy-hand interaction has focused on microgestures and motion-based techniques, which rely on finger articulation or relative movement. In situations where a stable grasp is required, such as handling fragile, heavy, or precision objects, such motion can be undesirable or impractical. Pressure-based input offers a complementary modality that enables interaction without changing finger pose, yet its use while holding objects has received limited empirical attention. To explore this, we conducted two within-subject experiments examining users’ ability to perform controlled pressure selections and analyzing finger-specific performance across different grasps and geometries. Results indicate that participants can reliably perform pressure-based selections in these conditions, achieving high success rates (92.7% on average) with low selection times (1.74s on average). Our findings characterize the potential of pressure input as a complementary microinteraction modality under grasp-constrained, busy-hand scenarios.

Touch interaction on everyday surfaces has long been envisioned as an extension of mixed-reality input, offering tactile feedback and proprioceptive cues that enhance user comfort and precision. However, most existing mixed-reality touch-sensing techniques are designed for static, dry, and large surfaces, making them unsuitable for real-world use where surfaces may be handheld, wet, or smaller in size. We introduce HaloTouch++, a mixed-reality touch input technique that enables low lift-off, water-tolerant and finger profile modified interactions on handheld surfaces. The system harnesses multi-path interference from time-of-flight depth sensing as a stable optical cue for detecting physical contact. A lightweight, plastic reflector attached to the surface amplifies these interference patterns, forming a distinctive “Halo” signature around touch points that remains consistent across surfaces and under varying poses and moisture conditions. In a 15-participant evaluation spanning multiple materials, user poses, and water conditions, HaloTouch++ achieved 97.3% touch-down accuracy and 93.3% gesture recognition accuracy.

Virtual Reality (VR) offers the potential for productivity work by providing expansive workspaces anywhere, yet supporting bare-hand interaction with multiple 2D windows remains challenging. We present HandPad, an asymmetric bimanual interaction framework that combines differentiated hand roles, self-haptic interaction, and hand remapping for multi-window interaction. The non-dominant hand sets a spatial frame, selects the interaction context, and provides a self-haptic surface, while the dominant hand performs on-hand touch and complementary mid-air manipulation relative to that frame. HandPad organizes interaction into three modes supporting cross-window navigation, within-window content manipulation, and application-window management. It also remaps the physical hands to virtual windows, allowing users to interact from more flexible physical postures regardless of window location. An exploratory study suggests that HandPad provides coherent interaction workflows, while revealing design tradeoffs between on-hand and mid-air interaction, informing the design of future bimanual interfaces for multi-window VR workspaces.

documents.abstract: Health and care settings present high-stakes contexts where it is essential that decision-making and access to information are timely and accurate. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools is increasingly influencing practice, while also introducing risks and challenges that can affect the safety, fairness, and trustworthiness of AI systems in these settings. This workshop critically explores the use of AI tools in health and care settings through the prism of four dimensions: power, time, inclusion and emotions. It will explore how pushing the boundaries of scenarios on the edge can influence the lived experience of multiple stakeholders, including healthcare providers, caregivers, researchers, industry partners, and people accessing health and care services. Participants will share experiences of AI use in health and care settings, engage in scenarios that can be challenged by the four dimensions, and reflect on how technology design can be sensitised to address the risks and challenges raised by the four dimensions in situations on the edge.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Reflective practice helps learners make sense of early-career workplace experiences, but can be difficult to sustain amid ambiguity, vulnerability, and pressure to present oneself competently. As AI tools are proposed as scalable supports, their implications for learner authority remain underexplored. This study examined AI-supported reflection in early-career workplace learning through a two-week design probe with five tertiary students and recent graduates undertaking placements, internships, or graduate programs. Participants completed spoken, written, structured, and AI-mediated reflection activities alongside mood tracking. Data comprised probe artefacts, AI outputs, and interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis and a multidimensional framework. Participants valued AI for organising thoughts, offering perspectives, and supporting communication, but resisted it when AI authored reflections, inferred emotions, or interpreted meaning. We propose conditional scaffolding: AI supports reflection when learners retain authority over meaning-making. We discuss implications for flexible scaffolds, bounded AI roles, temporal pattern visibility, and connections to human reflection.

Household intentions to invest in renewable energy sources (RESs) are associated with expected economic benefits, individual decision-making competencies, and perceived investment risk. The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools also raises the question of whether AI-supported decision-making modifies these relationships. This study examines the associations between economic motivations, entrepreneurial competencies, perceived financial risk, and RES investment intention and tests the potential moderating role of energy-related AI use. A cross-sectional CAWI survey was conducted among 563 adults involved in household expenditure, investment, or energy-related decisions in Poland. Hierarchical multiple regression with interaction terms was applied following an assessment of measurement reliability and validity. Economic motivations showed the strongest positive association with investment intention (β = 0.402; p < 0.001), entrepreneurial competencies showed a smaller positive association (β = 0.105; p = 0.009), and perceived financial risk was negatively associated with investment intention (β = −0.180; p < 0.001), supporting H1a–H1c. Energy-related AI use was rare, with only 35 respondents (6.2%) reporting at least one such activity. An additional exploratory comparison showed that early users of AI in energy-related decisions had substantially higher AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, and perceived usefulness of AI and were markedly younger than non-users, while they did not differ significantly in prior RES experience or investment intention. Neither the MOT × AI nor ENT × AI interaction was statistically significant, while the RISK × AI interaction was positive but did not reach the predefined significance threshold (B = 0.286; p = 0.061). Sensitivity and power analyses indicated that restricted variability in AI use limited the ability to reliably detect small interaction effects. The findings indicate a substantial gap between general AI use and its domain-specific application in household energy decisions. The study contributes by identifying characteristics associated with early AI-supported energy decision-making and by testing, without confirming, AI moderation under conditions of very limited domain-specific adoption.

documents.abstract: Human oversight is widely required for autonomous and artificial-intelligence systems, yet assigning a human role does not establish that the person can influence a hazardous trajectory. This study develops a bounded Safety-Control Governance Framework for assessing whether documentary human-control claims are operationally inspectable. Drawing on systems-theoretic safety, supervisory control, situation awareness, resilience engineering, meaningful human control, and AI governance, the framework distinguishes seven operational functions—authority allocation, feedback and observability, situational comprehension, intervention timing, safe-state objective, escalation, and recovery—and two cross-cutting governance functions: accountability assignment and documentation or assurance. The framework was applied to a purposive corpus of 24 public documents spanning autonomous mobility, maritime autonomy, drones and emergency operations, and high-risk AI or command support, producing 216 document–function observations. Authority and accountability were Explicit in 20 of 24 documents and documentation or assurance in 23 of 24. Explicit specification was less frequent for intervention timing (8 of 22 known cases), safe-state objectives (7 of 23), escalation (10 of 24), and recovery (6 of 24). Documentary families supplied complementary evidence, while configuration analysis located distinct discontinuities, including explicit authority while feedback and comprehension were not both Explicit in ten documents. Most degradation-pattern evidence was anticipatory or prescriptive rather than event-based. These numerical profiles are conditional on the final coding rules and source selection. The framework provides an evidence-linked protocol for tracing documentary control gaps; it does not assess operational performance.

Maritime accidents arise from interactions among people, work organisation, technology and the operating environment. Although casualty analyses frequently code human-related contributors, these classifications should not be interpreted as evidence that individual seafarers are the predominant root cause of accidents. This integrative narrative review therefore examines human factors as manifestations of a wider socio-technical system. A structured two-layer review strategy was used. Twenty maritime-focused empirical, review and analytical sources formed the core evidence corpus, while supplementary theoretical and cross-domain sources were used only to interpret mechanisms and transfer preventive lessons. The core synthesis identified four recurring patterns: fatigue and cognitive strain are shaped by scheduling, recovery opportunities, noise and automation demands; communication problems in multinational crews extend beyond language to authority gradients and shared mental models; reporting behaviour is strongly conditioned by organisational climate, commercial pressure and regulatory implementation; and many apparently individual errors emerge from interactions across cognitive, team, organisational, technical and environmental levels. HFACS, the Swiss Cheese Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Groupthink Theory, Error Management Theory, Rasmussen’s socio-technical perspective and Safety-II are therefore treated as complementary interpretive lenses rather than competing explanations. A preventive diagnostic matrix is proposed to connect analytical level, observable risk conditions, assessment indicators and upstream interventions. The review argues that maritime safety management should move away from worker-centred error correction toward primary prevention that redesigns work, technology, leadership and reporting systems around the conditions that shape safe performance.

Managers in nonprofit and non-governmental organisations increasingly receive advice from artificial intelligence tools when they forecast demand, allocate staff and budgets, screen applications, prioritise programmes and assess risk. The central management question is no longer whether such advice is available but how human judgement should be combined with it. This conceptual paper develops a calibrated-judgement framework for AI-assisted management decisions. It builds on two experimental literatures that point in different directions. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey report that people became less likely to rely on an algorithm after seeing it err, even when it outperformed a human forecaster. Alon-Barkat and Busuioc, in three experiments in the Netherlands, found no evidence of automation bias but found stronger adherence to advice aligned with group stereotypes in one study, with no significant difference between algorithmic and human-expert advice. These findings are connected to research on accountability and advice rationales, conditions for intuitive expertise, complacency and automation bias, decision structures and the automation–augmentation paradox. The framework holds that reliance on AI advice should be calibrated to the predictability of the decision environment, the reasons given for advice and the accountability that attaches to the decision. Six propositions address advice rationales, track records, selective adherence, workload, decision structure and skill preservation. No original empirical data are presented.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive trade analytics, and multimodal generative models into multinational enterprise (MNE) operations has fundamentally disrupted the foundational assumptions of International Business (IB) higher education. Traditional IB pedagogy—anchored in static comparative advantage models, retrospective case analyses, and isolated cross-cultural taxonomies—increasingly fails to prepare graduates for an era defined by algorithmic global value chains and geopolitical fragmentation. Moving beyond superficial classroom tool adoption, this study investigates how Artificial Intelligence can systematically restructure International Business education through the theoretical lenses of Institutional Entrepreneurship, Distributed Cognition, and Experiential Learning Theory. We argue that modern global business education must cultivate Symbiotic Cross-Border Intelligence—the integrated capacity to deploy, audit, and ethically govern intelligent systems across divergent sovereign, cultural, and regulatory jurisdictions. To operationalize this paradigm, the paper constructs an Adaptive Curriculum Co-Evolution Model paired with a Four-Tiered Experiential Learning Ecosystem that replaces passive lecturing with live cross-border algorithmic sandboxes, regulatory friction wargames, and multilingual stakeholder simulations. Drawing upon multi-semester pedagogical implementations across international finance, global supply chain resilience, and emerging-market entry courses, we demonstrate substantial improvements in students’ causal systems reasoning, hallucination forensics, and cross-cultural communicative agility. Finally, the paper addresses structural risks—including algorithmic monoculture, epistemic dependency, and extraterritorial data governance violations—and formulates an institutional compliance charter for business schools navigating the intelligent transformation of global commerce.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to support intrusion detection and threat investigation. However, accurate predictions and explainable outputs do not necessarily lead to appropriate human reliance: analysts may over-rely on incorrect recommendations or unnecessarily reject reliable ones. This work proposes a human-centric trust-calibrated framework that integrates an AI-driven Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), online estimation of analyst trust and cognitive load, and adaptive explanation selection within a closed-loop security interface. The NIDS combines traffic and textual threat representations to provide threat predictions, calibrated reliability estimates, and semantic evidence. Behavioral and interaction signals are processed through a probabilistic state-space model to estimate the analyst state, while a reliability-aware controller dynamically adjusts explanation depth and evidence granularity according to the Trust-Calibration Error (TCE), which captures the mismatch between inferred analyst trust and current NIDS reliability. Rather than treating trust estimation or calibration as standalone objectives, we investigate whether their integration improves operational human–AI performance under varying NIDS reliability. A controlled SOC-oriented evaluation compares the proposed trust-calibrated policy with static and trust-agnostic adaptive explanation strategies in terms of analyst decision quality, inappropriate reliance, investigation efficiency, and cognitive workload. Empirical evaluation across 2160 trials with 36 participants demonstrates that the proposed trust-calibrated policy improves decision accuracy from 81.4% to 89.3%, corresponding to an increase of 7.9 percentage points, curtails Automation Bias Rate (ABR) from 43.1% to 22.2% (31/72 to 16/72, representing a 48.4% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 21.8%, a 49.4% reduction), and decreases Inappropriate Rejection Rate (IRR) from 18.8% to 11.0% (122/648 to 71/648, representing a 41.8% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 18.9% to 10.9%, a 42.3% reduction), while lowering trust miscalibration error from 0.184 to 0.101. Crucially, these reliance gains are accompanied by a reduction in subjective workload from 58.4 to 48.7 on the NASA-TLX scale and a decrease in mean investigation time from 30.2 s to 28.1 s. These findings indicate that effective human-centered security interfaces should not maximize trust or explanation richness, but dynamically promote reliance that is consistent with the actual competence of the AI system.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot are now part of students’ everyday academic work. They help students understand concepts, write and debug programs and prepare assignments, but many students now ask AI for a direct answer before attempting a problem themselves. This raises a real concern about what happens to their ability to analyse information, reason and solve problems independently. This research proposes a framework for studying the relationship between Generative AI dependency and the critical thinking practices of students of computer applications. It follows a descriptive and correlational design and presents a structured questionnaire covering usage patterns, an eight-item dependency scale, a ten-item critical thinking practice scale and a verification scale. Composite scores classify students into low, moderate and high levels, and Cronbach's alphalpha, Spearman's rank correlation and the chi-square test are used to test three hypotheses. A review of recent studies shows that AI supports critical thinking when students question and verify its output, while over-reliance is linked with weaker reflection and independent performance. The paper concludes that the effect of AI depends on how it is used: a personal attempt first, hints instead of full answers, and verification of AI output help preserve independent thinking. Recommendations are offered for students, teachers and institutions.

The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the marketing landscape, providing scalable efficiencies in ad creation. However, the consumer side of AI integration remains underexplored. Drawing on algorithm aversion theory, this research extends the literature by examining how consumer characteristics moderate the persuasive impact of AI- and human-designed ads. Across a pretest and six large-scale experimental studies involving 6,579 consumer evaluations in Japan, this research finds that advertisements with undisclosed AI authorship often outperform human-designed advertisements in enhancing ad perceptions of creativity, credibility, clarity, and mental imagery (i.e., stimulating vivid consumer imagination) and, consequently, increasing purchase intentions. However, AI-generated ads are less effective among consumers with more generative AI experience, higher education, greater product category involvement, and lower interest in science. In these consumer segments, human-designed ads often have the advantage. These findings extend algorithm aversion theory by providing indirect evidence consistent with an implicit mechanism through which consumer characteristics trigger implicit algorithm detection (i.e., sensing algorithmic markers) and implicit algorithm aversion (i.e., subconscious devaluation of perceived artificiality) without requiring explicit disclosure of AI authorship. The findings inform marketing practice by emphasizing the importance of consumer segmentation.

This paper examines, from a theoretical and methodological perspective, the inclusive and sustainable educational opportunities offered by the use of an artificial intelligence assistant to develop the design competencies of students enrolled in Technological Education programmes in a digital learning environment. It analyses the informational and advisory functions of an AI chatbot in addressing students' individual information needs, supporting the use of vocationally oriented learning materials, and facilitating independent project-based activities. The paper also substantiates the didactic conditions for using an artificial intelligence assistant while preserving students' autonomy.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: The popularization of agents, models, and tools incorporating artificial intelligence is a phenomenon that has recently mobilized social and educational spheres due to new ethical and academic considerations, as well as the difficulties that arise when designing and evaluating learning experiences. The purpose of this study was to characterize the meaning and assess the scope of references to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in teacher training programs for secondary education in Uruguay, within the current curriculum (Plan 2023). The study focuses on STEM-related specialties. Through a content analysis of 156 curricular documents, the context of AI references was quantified and interpreted. The results show that these references are given a more instrumental than critical meaning. The presence of the Computer Science Teacher Training specialty is relevant, given that the interdisciplinary nature of the STEM approach can contribute to deepening critical thinking, transversality, and curricular flexibility for the pedagogical inclusion of these emerging technologies in teacher training.

Objective: To examine burnout rates among nursing professionals reported in publications from 2022 to 2026, considering measurement differences, associated factors, and implications for care. Methods: A descriptive narrative literature review based on scientific studies and reviews published within the defined period. Results: A 2023 meta-analysis estimated a global burnout prevalence of 30.0% (95% CI: 26.0–34.0%). A 2025 umbrella review reported a pooled prevalence of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for reduced personal accomplishment. A Brazilian study published in 2026 involving 3,594 nursing workers identified moderate exhaustion in 42.29% of participants; this indicator should not be interpreted as an overall syndrome prevalence. Conclusion: Burnout is a major occupational health concern, and heterogeneous measurement approaches require cautious interpretation and organizational prevention.

This paper examines industrial architecture and worker safety through a multidisciplinary architectural lens. It considers workflow, daylight, ventilation, ergonomics, and hazard prevention, while linking design choices to user experience, environmental performance, material responsibility and project delivery. The discussion synthesises established architectural literature, design guidance and recognised standards rather than presenting a new empirical survey. It argues that context-sensitive analysis, inclusive design, coordinated technical decisions and post-occupancy evaluation are essential to credible architectural outcomes. The paper concludes with practical directions for design teams and identifies the need for project-specific evidence before generalising strategies across climates, building types or communities.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Competency-based education and training (CBET) requires graduates to apply knowledge, perform occupational tasks, solve practical problems, and exercise professional judgement in authentic work environments. This narrative review examined the meaning and educational significance of practicum, the relationship between classroom learning and workplace competence, potential implementation barriers, relevant international experiences, and strategies for strengthening practicum in Tanzania’s livestock training system. The review synthesised literature and documentary information on workplace learning, agricultural and technical training, and apprenticeship approaches in Tanzania and selected countries. The findings distinguish theoretical instruction, institution-based practical training, field activities, and structured workplace practicum as complementary but non-equivalent learning experiences. Effective practicum requires clearly defined learning outcomes, authentic occupational tasks, supervised participation, constructive feedback, documented learning, and competency-based assessment. The synthesis identified potential implementation barriers, including inadequate financing, limited placement opportunities, unclear institutional and employer responsibilities, insufficient supervisor preparation, safety and safeguarding concerns, and weak assessment arrangements. International and Tanzanian apprenticeship examples highlighted transferable principles of employer engagement, shared training responsibilities, structured supervision, and quality assurance. However, available evidence does not establish the prevalence of these barriers or the adequacy of practicum across all Tanzanian livestock training institutions. The review proposes a coordinated framework integrating curriculum alignment, approved placement hosts, progressive competency development, student protection, sustainable financing, employer partnerships, and continuous monitoring. Tanzania should establish context-sensitive practicum standards, assess institutional readiness, strengthen collaboration between training institutions and livestock-sector employers, and pilot and evaluate implementation before wider adoption. National empirical research is also needed to establish baseline conditions and assess practicum quality and outcomes. Institutionalising structured practicum could strengthen the relevance of livestock education and support graduate preparedness for employment

This paper examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies into language teaching. It explores their role in developing vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, writing, and independent learning. The study adopts a literature review approach and uses the SAMR model to discuss technology integration in education. It also highlights challenges such as the reliability of AI-generated feedback, learners’ dependence on AI tools, and unequal access to digital resources. The paper emphasizes that effective technology integration requires clear learning objectives, teacher guidance, and meaningful communication. It concludes that AI and digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, teachers in language education.

This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies can be integrated into English for Specific Purposes (ESP) reading instruction using discipline-specific texts. The problem addressed is the mismatch between the linguistic and conceptual demands of authentic professional materials and learners’ varying levels of reading proficiency. A qualitative, literature-based methodological design was employed, combining thematic synthesis of established ESP and reading scholarship with instructional design analysis. The principal result is a three-stage framework linking pre-reading preparation, guided while-reading analysis and post-reading transfer to specific AI-supported teacher actions and observable learning evidence. A worked example demonstrates implementation with a professional text and identifies safeguards for accuracy, privacy and learner autonomy. The framework is a proposed pedagogical model, not an experimentally validated intervention. The article concludes that AI is most useful when it supports purposeful reading, disciplinary meaning-making and teacher-led formative assessment rather than replacing authentic engagement with texts.

In the 21st century, soft skills such as communication, critical thinking, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence are essential for personal and professional development. Unlike academic knowledge, they enhance the practical impact of what a person knows. As artificial intelligence (AI) develops rapidly, integrating it into education, and specifically into soft skills development, may accelerate learning. However, few existing solutions bring these skills together in a single system. Many learners prioritize academic knowledge because soft skills are not formally assessed and do not lead to a diploma. As a result, these skills are often neglected, although employers increasingly expect them in both international and domestic settings. This article explores how soft skills development can be combined in a single AI-based system. The pilot study draws on a survey of some respondents. The analysis examines how respondents currently use AI to develop soft skills, which skills they consider the most important and the most difficult to develop, and whether attitudes differ by age or occupation.

Recognising the challenges that international students face in integrating the Portuguese Education System, NOVA University launched a semester-long Foundation Program in 2017. Within this program, we introduced the Ideas Club course in 2020 to promote students’ engagement and facilitate long-term academic success. This paper examines whether and how the course has helped these students overcome cultural barriers and adapt to the European context. European issues serve as a guiding framework to help non-European students interact and discuss in constructive ways, thereby grasping the complexities of European reality. The course adopts a dialogic pedagogical approach, promoting student-led discussions on diverse topics while encouraging consciousness, critical reflection, and the dismantling of some stereotypes. Literature in international foundation education highlights the importance of self-determination theory in fostering intrinsic motivation, which is essential for the desired engagement and academic success. We show in this paper how the Ideas Club contributes to fostering intrinsic motivation.
topics: Education and experiences of immigrants and refugees

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming learning. This review examines how Generative AI can be integrated with established learning style models (VARK, Kolb, Felder-Silverman, and Honey & Mumford) to support student engagement in large online classes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) and included 41 studies that met the eligibility criteria. The review maps Generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences, synthesizes existing implementations, highlights benefits and challenges, and proposes pathways for future research and practice. Despite ongoing debates regarding the empirical validity of learning styles, Generative AI enables flexible, multimodal, and real-time adaptation. This study offers practical insights for educators and developers seeking to build more effective, learner centered learning systems
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: Interactive multimedia and educational games offer opportunities for elementary learning, but their mechanisms and outcome measures are heterogeneous.Aims: To synthesize the design features of interactive multimedia game-based learning (MMI-GBL), the evidence on student engagement, the implications for problem solving, and the methodological limitations of the field.Methods: This systematic literature review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting principles with descriptive mapping and narrative synthesis. A previously compiled 41-reference bibliography was reconciled into a retrospectively defined core set of 17 publications (2022–2026) and 24 supporting references. Core sources comprise seven empirical studies and ten secondary syntheses. Data were entered into a structured extraction matrix and appraised qualitatively by context and outcome construct.Results: Five empirical publications concern elementary or early elementary learners, including one complementary multimedia study, and address mathematics learning, task solving, computing terminology, and engagement. Recurring design features include coherent multimedia representations, explicit goals and missions, adaptive scaffolding, specific feedback, and opportunities to retry and reflect. Designs in which scaffolding and feedback prompted learners to choose strategies, explain, and revise were associated with learning and engagement gains, whereas rewards detached from reasoning contributed little. Behavioral and cognitive engagement were the dimensions most often evidenced; emotional and agentic engagement were rarely measured. Perceived usefulness or achievement does not directly measure problem-solving performance, and external meta-analytic estimates remain contextual.Conclusion: MMI-GBL is most effective when multimedia features, game mechanics, scaffolding, feedback, and teacher facilitation are aligned with meaningful learning activities. Further elementary-level research is needed to strengthen evidence on engagement and problem-solving outcomes.

Troubleshooting in operational environments relies on expert knowledge that is often undocumented and highly contextual. Informal data sources, such as communication logs, may hold some of this information, but their unstructured nature makes interpretation challenging. In a preliminary case study with a telescope operations facility, we explored whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct troubleshooting strategies from chat logs. LLM outputs were compared against those produced by a novice human analyst by two expert evaluators. We also compared an LLM with additional technical information in the context window and LLM outputs augmented by another novice analyst. While the domain experts varied in their scoring, overall LLM-generated analyses were judged as higher quality and more accurate than human-produced outputs. Neither additional technical context nor human augmentation resulted in meaningful improvements. These preliminary findings suggest LLMs show promise for expert knowledge extraction and decision-support in operational environments.

Sexting is relatively common behavior among adolescents, yet it raises parental concerns as it may pose substantial risks, particularly when occurring with unknown individuals met online. While parental mediation strategies are often recommended to mitigate such risks, longitudinal evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. To address this gap, our four-wave longitudinal study examines the impact of active and restrictive parental mediation on adolescents’ sending and receiving sexually-oriented online messages, including sexting, with people met online. We also examined adolescents’ age and gender as moderators. We analyzed data from 3,087 Czech adolescents (age M = 13.47, SD = 1.74, 50.1% male) using random intercept cross-lagged panel model. This approach advances understanding of the bidirectional dynamics between parenting and adolescent online sexual risk behaviors. Results show that active mediation was connected to lower sending and receiving such messages on a between-person level. However, on a within-person level, patterns were inconsistent. Increases in active mediation sometimes predicted higher receiving six months later, particularly among older adolescents, but effect was not stable, and no such effects were found for sending. In contrast, restrictive mediation was unrelated to sexting on a between-person level but showed some within-person effects, as at T2 higher restrictions predicted less sending and receiving at T3. Our results show that parental mediation has complex and context-dependent effects. Active mediation seems to reflect the overall communication climate within a family, rather than serving as a direct tool for changing behavior. These findings shift attention from parental mediation as a direct behavior-control strategy toward the broader role of developmentally sensitive family communication in helping adolescents navigate online sexual experiences.

The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is accelerating the transformation of digital society from “tool-based application” to “intelligent collaboration,” creating demand for composite competencies in technical operation, ethical awareness, and human–AI collaboration. To address limitations in existing digital literacy frameworks, particularly their inadequate treatment of cognitive overload, ethical risks, and disparities in the depth of GAI use, this study proposes the concept of “digital-intelligence literacy” (DIL) and constructs a comprehensive five-dimensional evaluation framework comprising Data-Inquisitive, Synergistic-Adaptive, Digital-Content-Hermeneutic, Ethico-Security, and Solution-Application literacies. Using 667 stratified random survey samples from Zhejiang Province, China, and employing principal component analysis, one-way ANOVA, structural equation modeling (SEM), and LASSO regression, this study systematically examines the current status, group disparities, and underlying mechanisms of DIL. The findings reveal the following: significant disparities in DIL across age groups, education levels, and GAI usage frequency, with older adults and low-frequency users encountering prominent challenges; GAI cognition emerges as the most critical factor for improving DIL, substantially exceeding the influence of attitudes and environmental perceptions; a core competency transformation chain of “Synergistic-Adaptive → Digital-Content-Hermeneutic → Solution-Application” literacy revealed by SEM, alongside dynamic interaction between safety-ethics and technological exploration; and participation intentions in DIL-related education are primarily driven by existing literacy levels, usage habits, and attitudes rather than cognitive factors alone. Based on these findings, this study proposes a “cognition-first, systemic-empowerment” strategy, including nationwide educational initiatives centered on GAI-based general knowledge and differentiated empowerment strategies for key groups, providing empirical evidence for local governments to formulate precise and inclusive literacy enhancement policies.

Artificial intelligence is often depicted in public discourse as either a compliant statistical instrument or an emerging entity endowed with knowledge, creativity, feelings, and intentions that may soon rival human capabilities. Both portrayals are fundamentally flawed, as they rely solely on observable performance and infer internal experiences from social appearances. This Viewpoint advocates for a more rigorous model: conceptualizing artificial intelligence as a modern seer, an intricate system that compresses, retrieves, and recombines recorded human knowledge at scales unattainable by any individual. The Viewpoint develops the seer from a metaphor into an analytical framework. The seer is a consulted but uncertified epistemic authority: its capabilities generate interaction cues, the cues invite inferences of understanding, emotion, intention, and authority, and governance must act on these cues and on the calibration of trust rather than on claims about a machine mind. This model clarifies both the practical utility of these systems and the misguided authority often attributed to them. It demonstrates that synthesis can generate novel insights without consciousness, that affective language can provide reassurance without genuine concern, and that value-sensitive recommendations can be produced without moral agency. These distinctions do not render the technology inherently safe, as systems lacking experience can still amplify errors, entrench biases, concentrate power, and undertake consequential actions. The field of drug development exemplifies these limitations: a model may integrate evidence throughout the pharmaceutical process; nevertheless, biological validation and accountable judgment remain essential. This discussion is no longer solely philosophical; regulatory bodies such as the United States Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, and prominent scientific publishers have each adopted frameworks to evaluate context, risk, credibility, and transparency, none of which directly address machine consciousness. Institutions have already moved beyond metaphor-based policymaking. This Viewpoint encourages scientists and scholars to do the same. It identifies ten misconceptions, eight category errors and two factual errors, traces each to the interaction cue that produces it, and states what the framework adds to existing debates on anthropomorphism, stochastic parrots, responsibility gaps, and context-based governance. Addressing these misconceptions will change how AI systems are tested, trusted, and governed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: When looking for a place to eat, how much do recommendations on your smartphone influence your choice? Can they help restaurants tucked away on side streets thrive in an age of algorithmic recommendations? We studied the launch of a location-based recommendation feature on South Korea’s largest search platform, tracking 16,720 restaurants over eight months. We find that visibility matters, but its benefits are uneven. Restaurants tucked away on side streets, far from subway stops, attracted the most additional attention when recommended by the algorithm. Yet this advantage did not translate into greater intentions to visit. Making a restaurant easier to discover did not necessarily overcome the inconvenience of reaching it. Digital information helped bridge this online-to-offline friction. Hard-to-reach restaurants with stronger online reputations and richer information, including customer reviews, photos, and menus, were better able to turn attention into visit intentions. For small businesses, visibility creates opportunities, but credible information helps turn attention into potential customers. For platforms and policymakers, location-based recommendations can bring overlooked businesses into view, but realizing their potential requires making reliable information readily available to consumers.

Understanding how users perform steering tasks on planar user interfaces (UIs) presented at oblique angles is important for designing effective interfaces in 3D workspaces such as VR, where the viewer’s angle relative to the content can vary. However, existing steering models have mainly assumed frontal viewing and do not fully account for viewpoint-dependent changes in apparent path geometry. We conducted a VR experiment in which users performed raycasting-based steering on circular paths displayed on a UI plane. We varied the oblique angle ϕ from 0° to 60°. We found that movement time generally increased as ϕ increased, and error rate was significantly higher at 60° than in the 0° , 20° , and 40° conditions. To model this effect, we extended the steering law using apparent path length, apparent width, and projected local curvature computed from the user’s viewpoint. A baseline steering model based only on geometric path length and width on the UI plane achieved an adjusted R 2 of 0.9024, whereas a viewpoint-dependent global steering model based on apparent path length and width achieved an adjusted R 2 of 0.9637. A local curvature-integrated steering model further improved the fit, achieving the highest adjusted R 2 of 0.9910 and the lowest AIC among the compared models. In leave-one-condition-out cross-validation, this model showed the best predictive performance among the compared models. These results show that incorporating how the appearance of geometry changes with the viewpoint improves steering-time prediction in our tested VR setup, which provides quantitative design guidance for spatially fixed UIs.

Although large corporations are increasingly implementing corporate volunteering as a strategic corporate social responsibility initiative, the psychological drivers of such participation remain underexplored. Drawing on self‐determination theory and the functional theory approach to volunteering, this study surveyed 440 nonmanagerial employees from medium‐ and large‐sized enterprises in Poland. Our goal was to investigate the link between the satisfaction and frustration of basic psychological needs at work and motivations for corporate volunteering. We used linear regression and latent profile analyses to test our hypotheses. The results showed that relatedness satisfaction was positively associated with all motives recognized by functional theory, except the social motive. Relatedness frustration was also positively related to the protective, career, and enhancement motives. Additionally, latent profile analysis identified three need satisfaction profiles (satisfied, autonomy‐frustrated, and relatedness‐and‐competence frustrated) that varied in their motives for corporate volunteering, except for career motive. We discuss the practical implications for employers and corporate managers interested in implementing or encouraging participation in corporate volunteering programs.

Purpose This study develops Sustainable Human Performance Work Systems (SHuPWS) to explain how HR systems can address the tensions created by integrating sustainability into strategic human resource management. Design/methodology A systematic review of 108 Scopus-indexed articles identifies recurring tensions, theoretical perspectives, and sustainability-oriented HR practices. The synthesis integrates stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, and the ability–motivation–opportunity framework across macro, meso, and micro levels. Findings Five interdependent tensions concern short- and long-term priorities, organisational performance and employee well-being, dualistic and paradoxical thinking, autonomy and standardisation, and business-oriented and values-based sustainability. SHuPWS are conceptualised as configurations of interdependent HR practices that connect economic, social and environmental objectives with employee well-being, voice, capability development and sustainable effort. Ability-, motivation- and opportunity-enhancing practices are proposed to influence short- and medium-term processes contributing to triple-bottom-line outcomes. These relationships vary across configurations, time horizons, and institutional and organisational conditions. Originality/value The study advances sustainable HRM research by identifying sustainability tensions within the design and operation of HR systems. The framework incorporates configurational, temporal and contextual variation into the explanation of system effects over time. It connects stakeholder expectations, organisational capabilities and employee experience within a multilevel account, and specifies relationships for subsequent empirical examination.

As generative AI becomes integrated into creative practice, understanding how creative agency is negotiated during human–AI collaboration has become a challenge for Human–Computer Interaction (HCI). This paper reports preliminary findings from a qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with three Filipino music producers who incorporate generative AI into their workflows. Inductive analysis identified negotiation moments through which participants determined where and how generative AI could participate and how AI-generated contributions should be evaluated, modified, and incorporated. We use negotiation moments as an emerging analytical lens for understanding how creators regulate AI participation while exercising creative agency. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous collaborator or passive tool, participants determined the scope of AI involvement and retained human judgment over how AI contributions became part of their work. These preliminary findings offer an HCI perspective on how creative AI systems might support human decision-making and creative control.

This conceptual study examines potential neurolinguistic mechanisms associated with generative artificial intelligence (GAI)-assisted academic writing and proposes a conceptual model centered on the proposed theoretical construct of syntactic offloading. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly support stages of scholarly text production, traditional cognitive boundaries between internal language generation and external computational support are being redrawn. Grounded in Levelt’s speech production model and Hagoort’s Memory–Unification–Control (MUC) framework, this research examines how delegating sentence construction, grammatical structuring, and discourse organization to AI affects working memory allocation, executive control, and language production networks. The paper conceptualizes syntactic offloading as a specialized form of cognitive offloading in which specific syntactic planning operations are partially transferred to AI systems, while the writer retains agency over conceptualization, critical evaluation, and communicative intent. Under the proposed account, syntactic offloading may redistribute rather than necessarily diminish overall cognitive engagement: working memory demands shift from low-level sentence generation to high-level evaluation, source integration, and scientific verification. Concurrently, executive control functions such as attentional regulation, inhibitory control, and metacognitive monitoring become paramount in assessing AI-generated outputs for conceptual precision, methodological validity, and stylistic alignment. The article further discusses the possible neuroplastic implications of sustained reliance on AI sentence formulation, considering whether long-term syntactic offloading may alter the functional engagement of neural pathways (e.g., Broca’s area (Brodmann area 44, BA44)) responsible for independent syntactic processing. Ultimately, the study frames AI-assisted academic writing as a distributed, bidirectional interaction between human cognition and computational support. It emphasizes the necessity of maintaining human critical oversight to preserve authorial voice and scholarly rigor while leveraging AI for enhanced writing efficiency.

Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent. We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error. Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GAI) can support writing, but learners may respond differently to its guidance. This study examined whether field dependence–independence (FDI) moderated the effect of GAI guidance on critical thinking behaviors (CTB) during human–AI collaborative writing. In a mixed-design study, 65 journalism students completed news-writing tasks with Standard GAI, which provided direct responses, and Heuristic GAI, which elicited learners’ reasoning. We coded 696 user prompts as CTB or non-CTB and analyzed them with logistic generalized linear mixed-effects models. Heuristic GAI was associated with more CTB overall, but its effect decreased as GEFT scores increased: students toward the field-dependent end showed larger increases in CTB and greater uptake of cognitive guidance. Source-specific analyses located this heterogeneity primarily in learners’ uptake of cognitive guidance; neither the condition nor moderation effect was significant for learner-initiated CTB. The findings support learner-sensitive GAI scaffolding in educational HCI.

documents.abstract: Critical organizations, whose missions involve producing social critique, such as academic, journalistic, and activist organizations, face what we term a dilemma of “critical positionality,” meaning that they must respond to contradictory demands for critical proximity and distance. This dilemma arises because legitimate critique must remain “close to the ground” to access “lived experiences” yet also adopt sufficient distance from practice to allow for problematization. Critical positionality is an organizational challenge that is exacerbated during moments of digital transitions, when proximity and distance are reconfigured through transmediality—that is, movement of content across media types—which can disrupt organizational practices oriented toward critical positionality. To understand how organizations navigate digital transmediality to maintain their critical positions, we studied a Brazilian progressive news outlet during a digital transition. Organizational attempts to build proximity to users were followed by a reactive attempt at repositioning, which cascaded into further efforts to stabilize a position consistent with the organization’s critical mission. By analyzing approximation and distancing dynamics, we contribute to understanding critical positionality in practice, discussing how critique is shaped by evolving requirements of digital transmediality, and illustrating organizational tensions developed in this process in a critical news outlet.

documents.abstract: Introduction When students feel that generative artificial intelligence (AI) agrees with them, do they remain willing to acknowledge possible error and seek evidence against their own views? We distinguished AI support for an answer from teacher support for questioning an answer. We examined how perceived AI agreement and teacher support for reasoned dissent relate to state intellectual humility and reported counterevidence seeking. Methods We surveyed 386 undergraduates, mainly first-year students, at one vocational and technical university. Students completed the questionnaire in class after an AI-assisted English learning task. A separate pilot sample informed the measurement model. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling examined the associations, with bootstrap intervals for indirect associations. Results In the main model, perceived AI agreement and teacher support were positively associated with intellectual humility. Humility was positively associated with reported counterevidence seeking. The estimated indirect associations involving humility were positive for both predictors. Their bootstrap intervals excluded zero, with no clear difference between the two estimates. Neither direct path was statistically significant in the main model. Discussion These initial findings suggest that perceived support for one’s view and encouragement to question claims should be considered together when examining humility and counterevidence seeking in AI-assisted learning.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has changed how brands communicate with consumers through personalized recommendations, automated responses, and algorithm-driven content on social media. However, favorable evaluations of these interactions may not directly translate into purchasing intentions or positive brand perceptions. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI-enabled social media intelligence quality and sustainable brand perception through the sequential mediating roles of consumer digital trust, electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM) intention, and purchase intention. Data were collected from 250 Indonesian social media users and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that AI-enabled social media intelligence quality is positively associated with digital trust and e-WOM intention. Digital trust is positively associated with e-WOM intention, but its direct relationship with purchase intention is not statistically significant. Both e-WOM intention and purchase intention are positively associated with sustainable brand perception. The hypothesized sequential indirect effect is statistically significant (β = 0.028, p = 0.001). From an information systems perspective, these findings provide empirical evidence linking perceived AI-mediated communication quality to psychological, social, behavioral, and perceptual responses. The study suggests that evaluations of AI-enabled communication systems should consider user trust and recommendation intentions alongside prospective commercial outcomes. Keywords—AI-enabled social media intelligence, digital trust, electronic word-of-mouth, purchase intention, sustainable brand perception, sequential mediation.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: This article analyzes the possibilities of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies into foreign language instruction and personalizing the educational process in higher and secondary special education institutions. The study examines the advantages of adaptive learning platforms, generative language models (LLMs), and automated assessment systems tailored to students' language proficiency levels, learning paces, and individual needs. Furthermore, practical recommendations and methodological approaches for the step-by-step integration of AI tools into the educational framework are presented.

There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

AI‐enabled carbon management is reshaping the hospitality industry, but its promise depends on a workforce that can combine digital fluency with critical ESG judgment. To address this need, this study develops and tests a framework linking ESG‐oriented mindful technology engagement (EMTE) and generative AI capability to five dimensions of digital carbon technology literacy and perceived sustainable carbon achievement (PSCA). We analyzed survey data from 174 hospitality undergraduates in Taiwan using a two‐stage higher‐order PLS‐SEM approach. EMTE and generative AI capability were positively associated with all five dimensions. However, generative AI capability selectively attenuated the EMTE–evaluation relationship, while the other four interactions were not supported. In the direct‐path model, design, ethics, and vision were positively associated with PSCA. By conceptualizing EMTE as a mindfulness‐informed technology‐engagement composite and digital carbon literacy as a multidimensional capability, the study advances a contingent view of human–AI collaboration and highlights verifying AI‐assisted work as a priority for pre‐entry ESG human capital development.

Understanding the extent to which employees perceive organizational outcomes as fair is crucial in explaining employee attitudes and organizational behaviours. However, while the literature on distributive justice primarily focuses on the outcomes of employees' fairness evaluations regarding pay, rewards, and other organizational outcomes, the extent to which employee control over how the work is performed shapes these evaluations has been relatively less examined. The aim of this research is to examine the predictive relevance of employees' level of control over their work on their perceptions of distributive justice. The research was conducted using data obtained from 246 white-collar and blue-collar employees. In measuring job control, Dwyer and Ganster's (1991) job control approach was utilized, and elements of job control related to task variety, task execution order, work pace, task scheduling, work methods and procedures, and the arrangement of the physical work environment were measured. In the study, a supervised machine-learning classification framework based on nested cross-validation was applied. According to the analysis, among the components of job control, the autonomy to determine the amount of work an individual will do may be informative in distinguishing evaluations of distributive justice. In addition, predicting how decisions will turn out, interacting with people, deciding on the source of information, and job control over wages may help differentiate the evaluations of distributive justice. Organizational tenure has emerged as a potentially relevant contextual predictor carrying predictive information in terms of distributive justice evaluations. The research positions job control as a potential organizational resource linked to distributive justice evaluations; it also offers a methodological contribution to the use of machine learning-based classification in organizational behaviour research. In terms of application, the findings suggest that increasing employees’ control over work processes can contribute to strengthening the perception of justice within organizations.

BACKGROUND: Reliance on AI-supported health recommendations is consequential, but a single behavioral source-selection decision is not equivalent to multidimensional psychological trust. Biosignals may contain predictive information before a choice, although small-sample multimodal models require leakage-free evaluation and cautious interpretation. PURPOSE: This study evaluated whether facial-expression probabilities and galvanic skin response (GSR) features predict a task-specific binary choice of an AI-labeled rather than doctor-labeled recommendation in a simulated ADHD assessment. The outcome is treated as a behavioral indicator of reliance rather than a direct measure of psychological trust. Method: This cross-sectional laboratory analysis included a cohort of 60 participants (40 AI-labeled and 20 doctor-labeled choices). Eight facial-expression probabilities and two GSR phasic features were evaluated in prespecified Early (6-3 s) and Proximal (3-0 s) windows. Ten repeats of participant-level stratified five-fold cross-validation were used. Scaling and SMOTETomek resampling occurred only within training folds, and the logistic stacking meta-learner was trained on strictly cross-fitted base-model probabilities. Model-specific 95% confidence intervals and paired AUC differences were estimated with 10,000 stratified participant bootstrap samples; five paired tests were Holm-adjusted. RESULTS: Early-window ROC-AUCs were 0.643 (95% CI 0.490-0.786) for Face, 0.430 (0.287-0.578) for GSR, and 0.526 (0.375-0.679) for stacking. Proximal-window ROC-AUCs were 0.550 (0.399-0.699), 0.381 (0.240-0.530), and 0.376 (0.229-0.529), respectively. Stacking did not outperform either modality. Early stacking was worse than Early Face (ΔAUC = -0.116, 95% CI -0.183 to -0.056; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002); the other adjusted paired comparisons were not significant. CONCLUSION: Multimodal stacking did not improve prediction in this small exploratory sample. These results do not establish either a general advantage or a lack of value of multimodal fusion. They do not support deployment or direct trust detection. Larger studies with verified synchronization, repeated decisions, independent trust measures, and external validation are required.

The inevitable integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English language teaching has transformed traditional approaches to writing instruction. Although AI offers numerous opportunities for improving students’ writing skills through immediate feedback, language correction, and personalized support, its increasing use raises concerns about students’ ability to think and work independently. In particular, excessive reliance on AI may reduce students’ active engagement in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their own writing. Therefore, the question is not whether AI should be integrated into EFL writing instruction, but how teachers can use it without weakening students’ metacognitive agency. Drawing on recent research, this paper discusses the importance of maintaining students’ responsibility for their learning and proposes the Metacognitive Agency Preservation and Development (MAPD) Framework. The framework introduces five stages of AI-assisted writing instruction aimed at encouraging independent thinking, critical evaluation, and reflective learning. It emphasizes that AI should support students throughout the writing process rather than replace their cognitive efforts. The paper concludes that the effective integration of AI requires a balance between technological assistance and students’ independent metacognitive development.

Automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being implemented in animal research, particularly through Automated Welfare Monitoring (AWM) systems designed to augment traditional human assessment of animal welfare. Among the most prominent examples are home cage monitoring technologies for continuous monitoring of rodents. Current ethical discussions surrounding AWM primarily focus on its contribution to the 3Rs principles (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), especially its potential to minimise harm through continuous welfare assessment and earlier interventions. However, the 3Rs alone do not fully address the broader ethical and social implications of automation and AI in animal research. AWM systems have the potential to reshape decision-making, responsibility, oversight, animal care jobs, and human-animal relationships within laboratory practice. In this article, we propose a complementary framework for the ethical implementation of AWM in animal research. Drawing on scholarship in bioethics and AI ethics, we propose five principles to guide the design, implementation, and governance of AWM systems: (1) Animal Welfare and 3Rs; (2) Human Autonomy and Accountability; (3) Fairness; (4) Transparency; and (5) Respect for Animals. We illustrate how these principles address ethical concerns arising from AWM, including the preservation of professional expertise and autonomy, equitable access across institutions and species, data governance and regulatory oversight, and the risks of objectifying animals through datafication. Rather than replacing the 3Rs, these principles extend them by addressing the ethical and social conditions under which automated systems are integrated into animal research, thereby supporting the responsible implementation of AWM while promoting animal welfare.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to environmental sustainability while causing environmental problems. From the perspective of adaptive governance, we ask what the governments of Japan and South Korea would have to learn from their publics at the initial stage of adaptation. Using a 2024 survey of 700 citizens in each country, we find public support for a firm-targeted subsidy and a tax, with the tax receiving more support in both countries. Support was associated with concern about climate change and AI, and with anticipated environmental effectiveness. Trust in government was associated with subsidy support in Japan; no other trust association survived sensitivity analysis. Anticipated negative economic impact was associated with stronger tax support, though on a different time horizon in each country. We argue that support reaches further toward coercive instruments than innovation-first governance assumes, and that learning from it would require institutionalized citizen inputs and information on policy effects.

In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. Building on his course, AI and Its Applications in the LIS Profession-- one of the few LIS offerings that comprehensively examines artificial intelligence and generative AI across libraries, archives, and museums; along with examining the historical, ethical, and sociopolitical dimensions of AI-- Simmons will highlight the importance of AI fluency in LIS, emphasizing practical, day-to-day applications for information professionals. He will introduce effective prompting strategies to support LIS workflows, including the TAP method (Think, Ask, Play), a framework he developed. Grounded in evidence-based iterative prompting this approach has produced positive outcomes through in-class experimentation with students. Laura Saunders teaches and writes in the areas of public services, reference, library instruction and information literacy. Drawing on scholarship and a critical pedagogy/ andragogy background, she will outline some AI skills and knowledge that might be important to address in these courses, explore how traditional skills such as the reference interview and neutral questioning remain relevant, and discuss how to highlight that continuity for students. She will also explore some of the pushback to AI content and share ideas for approaching AI assignments that preserves some student agency. Sarah Appedu is a PhD candidate whose dissertation research and teaching takes an agency and ethics-oriented approach to critically interrogating AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon. While access to AI tools and skills is often prioritized in many AI literacy initiatives, Sarah empowers librarians to ask the hard questions that go beyond issues of access and consider the ways in which AI can be in conflict with the very values we’re trained to embody. Her work aims to problematize the inevitability narratives surrounding AI use that are often perpetuated by the technology industry by centering librarians’ commitments to sustainability, the public good, equity, and intellectual freedom & property. She will present sets of critical questions related to each core value of librarianship that enable both technical knowledge of AI systems and agentic responses to their possibilities, limitations, and ethical consequences. The panelists will have several questions prompts prepared to help facilitate the conversation: Do LIS faculty have a need or obligation to integrate AI into their curricula? Why or why not? Have you experienced pressure either to integrate or to avoid AI in your teaching? Are you currently addressing AI in your teaching? If so, what activities, strategies or topics have you found to be effective? If not, what are your reasons for not addressing it? What are your experiences around student use of AI? What are your thoughts on AI inevitability and AI refusal? How can we navigate these tensions? The panel will be relevant to LIS instructors addressing or considering addressing AI in their curricula.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
