Digital transformation in Islamic higher education has driven fundamental changes in academic data management systems, particularly regarding the role of PDDIKTI operators in Private Islamic Higher Education Institutions (PTKIS). The shift toward technology-based administrative systems demands improvements in digital literacy, work motivation, and organizational readiness to support accurate, efficient, and sustainable data management. This study aims to reconstruct the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators through a needs-and-expectations approach in the digital era, while identifying the psychological, technological, and organizational factors influencing operator performance. This study employs a literature review method analyzing 20 scientific articles published between 2022 and 2026, utilizing literature collection, selection, thematic grouping, and qualitative descriptive synthesis stages. The results indicate that digital transformation through academic information systems, e-learning, Dapodik, and the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) enhances work efficiency, service quality, and data accuracy. However, challenges persist, including low digital literacy, high administrative workloads, technological adaptation needs, and suboptimal organizational support. This study contributes to the development of a conceptual model that integrates motivational, technological, and managerial aspects as a foundation for understanding the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators in the era of digital transformation at PTKIS. The limitation of this study lies in its use of a literature review approach, meaning empirical data do not yet support the findings. Therefore, future research is recommended to conduct quantitative or qualitative empirical testing in the field to validate this conceptual model and to explore the effectiveness of organization-based digital literacy training programs in greater depth.

Frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) has been used for contact sensing via vision, while repropagated FTIR (RFTIR) has enabled system miniaturization. However, conventional RFTIR-based methods cannot adequately handle overlapping contact images generated by multiple contacts. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach for estimating multiple contacts for multitouch sensing. Images resembling those captured by FTIR-based methods were reconstructed using pseudo-inverse ray tracing, and contact positions were then estimated based on these reconstructions. We evaluated the accuracy of multitouch sensing under various experimental conditions, and confirmed that the estimation was highly accurate, even with four contacts. Several applications were implemented to demonstrate the practicality of the proposed method, including single-sided and simultaneous double-sided multitouch sensing.

documents.abstract: Organisations increasingly combine employee-led job redesign with artificial intelligence (AI) to support adaptive work and performance. This study examines the relationships among job crafting (JC), self-reported AI use, and employee-reported performance-related outcomes in the UAE public sector. Primary cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 433 employees working in HRM departments of Dubai Government organisations. The study tests the direct associations of JC and AI with the outcome measure, the moderating role of AI in the JC-outcome relationship, and whether these relationships differ formally across gender and age groups. Regression results show positive associations for JC (β = 0.552, p < 0.001) and AI use (β = 0.166, p < 0.001). The AI × JC interaction is not significant (B = −0.024, t = −0.650, p = 0.516), indicating that AI does not strengthen the JC-outcome relationship in this sample. Formal interaction tests also do not establish significant differences in the focal relationships across gender or age groups. The findings suggest that job crafting and AI use may contribute independently to perceived performance-related outcomes, while their combination is not automatically synergistic. The study contributes to human-centred AI and job-crafting research in a public-sector setting, while explicitly recognising limitations arising from convenience sampling, cross-sectional self-report data, and the restricted content validity of the retained measurement composites. From a social sustainability perspective, these findings inform how employee autonomy and responsible AI use may support adaptable public-sector work practices and sustainable human resource management. The results highlight the importance of balancing digital transformation with employee agency, while not establishing long-term sustainability outcomes.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft replies to patient messages, but the methods available for evaluating such drafts were developed for other kinds of systems, and expert evaluators are difficult to recruit at the scale that LLM output requires. We propose Research through Evaluation (RtE), an iterative approach in which the evaluation metrics and the grading rubric are developed together with the clinicians who apply them. We applied RtE in a retrospective comparative study of 158 prostate cancer patient inquiries, comparing replies written by the clinical care team with replies generated by a GPT-4-based in-basket bot. Three rounds of human evaluation with clinical professionals (Rounds 1–3) were followed by a fourth round in which four LLM graders scored the same responses with the final rubric. Across the human rounds, the design moved from disclosed-source comparison to randomized single-blind grading, Conciseness was replaced by Clarity and Trustworthiness by Empathy, and items on editing effort and time to answer were added. In the final clinician evaluation, clinical care team replies scored higher on Completeness, Correctness and Clarity, in-basket bot replies scored higher on Empathy, and in-basket bot replies more often needed major editing. All four LLM graders rated the in-basket bot replies more favourably than the clinical care team replies, and their absolute agreement with one another was low (Krippendorff's alpha 0.07–0.18) compared with that of the clinician graders (0.53–0.81). RtE produced a documented evaluation instrument in which every revision can be traced to the round that prompted it, and the results indicate that zero-shot LLM graders cannot yet replace clinician evaluation in this setting.

documents.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in academic work, it is reshaping how researchers seek, interpret, and use information across scholarly activities (Andersen et al., 2025). At the same time, AI-generated information presents new challenges for credibility assessment because its reliability and suitability for academic tasks are not always readily apparent (Choi et al., 2025). This study examines how generative AI is incorporated into academic information practices and how people respond when its outputs remain uncertain. The semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 faculty members, graduate students, librarians, and academic support professionals working or studying in U.S. higher-education settings. An iterative thematic analysis showed that participants rarely treated generative AI as a self-contained information source. Instead, they moved between AI systems, scholarly resources, specialised tools, and human expertise as their tasks developed. Uncertainty often emerged when generated information appeared plausible but was difficult to substantiate, when participants lacked the expertise needed to judge an answer, or when AI involvement conflicted with their understanding of appropriate academic work. Participants responded by seeking corroborating evidence, revising how AI was used within a task, or turning away from it when further checking required too much effort or when they wished to retain personal judgement and authorship. Faculty and academic support professionals also described a broader responsibility for helping students and colleagues navigate these uncertainties through clearer expectations and critical guidance. The findings position generative AI within a wider academic information environment and show that its use is shaped by continuing judgements about when generated information is sufficient, when other resources are needed, and where human responsibility should remain.

documents.abstract: Amid the rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), this study investigates how integrating this technology into educational feedback processes can enhance learning experiences. Specifically, we investigate the potential of GenAI to complement peer feedback practices among 295 graduate students at a US-based university during the 2023 academic year. Employing an exploratory research design, the study gathered both quantitative and qualitative data through post-course surveys to address key research questions regarding the quality, usefulness, and actionability of peer and AI reviews, as well as their respective advantages and disadvantages. The findings reveal that, while peer reviews were slightly more favorably perceived across all dimensions, AI-generated feedback offered unique strengths, such as consistency and immediacy, which may enrich the feedback experience in distinct ways. The thematic analysis revealed distinct but complementary functions associated with each modality. This research underscores the importance of integrating human expertise with AI technology in feedback mechanisms. By illuminating how AI can augment, rather than replace, human feedback, we offer practical insights for educators, instructional designers, and policymakers seeking to enhance feedback experiences through emerging digital technologies.

Readers of the philosophical literature on artificial intelligence (AI) will encounter an unexpected word, one that medicine has carried for two and a half millennia: pharmakon. Revitalised by Derrida and elaborated by Bernard Stiegler into a general theory of technology, the figure has lately been carried over to generative AI to capture the simultaneous enhancement and diminishment of cognition this technology produces in its users. The present paper argues that when philosophy borrows this word it should borrow it in full, in the sense it has acquired since Plato. The phármakon of contemporary clinical medicine is a relational object whose therapeutic or toxic character emerges in a specified encounter between substance, subject, and context. Stiegler’s pharmacology is itself relational, locating ambivalence in the process of transindividuation; but it does not provide an operational vocabulary for specifying how effects vary systematically between individual subjects. Clinical pharmacology provides such a vocabulary. Its accumulated learning — pharmacokinetic variability, pharmacogenetic polymorphism, idiosyncratic susceptibility, drug–drug interaction, therapeutic window, tolerance, withdrawal, and expectancy effects — has cognitive analogues in human interaction with large language models (LLMs) that have not yet been developed into a coherent pharmacological vocabulary and that early empirical research is beginning to measure. The paper proposes a reframing from the generic to the respondent pharmakon, not as a refutation of Stiegler’s pharmacology but as its specification at a level where clinical, pedagogical, and policy decisions can be made.

Background Clinical agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can alter its actions during a clinical task, creating failure pathways that conventional performance metrics may not capture. Whether safeguards interrupt these pathways remains uncertain. Aim To map safeguard effects, residual failures, human recovery, and resource consequences in clinical agentic and related AI workflows. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, for English-language, peer-reviewed empirical journal reports. This scoping review used independent screening, duplicate extraction, narrative synthesis, and result-specific critical appraisal. Results The 111 reports comprised 56 functionally agentic, 29 related non-agentic, 22 architecture-uncertain, and four human-factors reports; 38 of the 56 agentic reports explicitly documented model-directed subsequent-action selection. Among the 111 selected appraisal results, none both isolated a specified safeguard’s effect and demonstrated reduced measured patient harm. Configurations incorporating safeguards improved selected outcomes, but gains coexisted with omissions, reduced sensitivity, false reassurance, delay, or transferred review burden. Concurrent changes in models, prompts, evidence access, and workflow frequently prevented attribution to individual controls. Some patient-randomised trials reported patient or process benefits, but evaluated bundled interventions rather than the contribution of a safeguard. Human authority was more often documented than successful error detection and recovery; requiring clinician approval did not establish that residual errors were recognised and corrected. Performance varied across models, settings, and information conditions, limiting transfer of favourable findings. Reported efficiency gains depended on measurement boundaries and did not consistently account for review, correction, escalation, and downstream work. Discussion The evidence exposes a gap between local error control and safety across a complete clinical episode. A safeguard can reduce a targeted error while shifting risk to later decisions or human reviewers. We propose a post hoc, non-ordinal evidence profile addressing mechanism fidelity, residual and introduced failures, robustness, joint human–AI performance, and clinical consequences. The profile requires validation; heterogeneous designs and retrospective methodological refinements constrain inference. Conclusion Clinical safety should be evaluated across the complete care pathway, tracing safeguard effects through residual error, human recovery, and patient-relevant outcomes. Selective autonomy requires joint assessment of residual risk and the capacity for timely human review.

documents.abstract: Occupational health risks are common among oil and gas dispensing workers, making safety training an important component of workplace health protection. This study examined the relationship between safety training and health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional research design was adopted, and data were collected from 212 oil and gas dispensing workers using a structured questionnaire. Safety training and health-seeking behaviour were measured using composite scores derived from Likert-type items. Descriptive statistics were used to assess the extent of safety training practices, while Pearson Product Moment Correlation and simple linear regression were employed to examine the relationship and predictive effect of safety training on health-seeking behaviour. The findings indicated a high level of safety training among the workers. A strong, positive and statistically significant relationship was found between safety training and health-seeking behaviour (r = .775, p < .001). Regression analysis further showed that safety training significantly and positively predicted health-seeking behaviour (B = 0.685, β = .776, t = 17.842, p < .001). The regression model was statistically significant, F(1, 210) = 318.354, p < .001, and explained 60.3% of the variance in health-seeking behaviour (R² = .603). The study concludes that higher levels of safety training are associated with more positive health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers. It recommends sustained and periodic safety training incorporating hazard recognition, preventive health practices, early reporting of health problems and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Practically, the study provides evidence for integrating health-seeking components into routine safety training, particularly early recognition and reporting of occupational health problems, preventive practices, and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Keywords: Safety training; Health-seeking behaviour; Occupational health; oil and gas workers; Calabar Metropolis.

documents.abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.

documents.abstract: Screen sharing in online conferencing can unintentionally expose private information on the presenter’s screen. Existing protections mainly rely on masking or blurring, which can disrupt context and interaction understanding. We propose a generative, semantic-aware replacement approach that substitutes sensitive regions with visually coherent content in dynamic screen environments. We implement two variants with different degrees of semantic grounding: Semantic-Element-Preserving Replacement (SEPR) and Semantic-Element-Agnostic Replacement (SEAR), and compare them with masking and blurring. In a video-based user study that isolates latency effects, we evaluate detectability, confidence of detection, perceived identifiability, and user experience from both screen-sharer and screen-viewer perspectives. SEAR significantly reduced detectability relative to masking, and also lowered perceived identifiability compared to blurring and SEPR. Replacement methods significantly improved context understanding and visual naturalness over masking, and SEAR also outperformed blurring in visual naturalness; for context preservation, SEAR was rated higher than masking, while the SEPR–masking comparison was near the significance threshold. Qualitative responses further revealed role-dependent concerns and a social risk of misinterpretation, motivating design implications for tuning semantic fidelity and signaling obfuscation intent.

As Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly make decisions and take actions for users, understanding how transparency shapes human–agent interaction is critical. We report a controlled study with 60 participants interacting with a policy-governed agent in a customer-service domain under three transparency conditions: opaque, partial, and transparent. The study shows greater transparency increased perceived understanding of agent behavior. However, it did not improve identification of silent failures, defined as plausible errors presented without warning. Partial transparency supported error detection more effectively than full transparency, suggesting that additional explanations do not necessarily enhance critical evaluation. Greater transparency was also associated with lower perceived agent steerability, reflecting reduced belief that outcomes could be influenced through altered response strategies. Participants challenged agent decisions less directly and engaged more with stated rules under transparent conditions. These findings highlight trade-offs between clarity, oversight, and user agency, motivating transparency designs that better support effective human oversight.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded in nursing students' routines, yet academic AI overreliance is rarely quantified, especially in resource-limited settings. Objective To examine the relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance among nursing students in the West Bank, Palestine. Methods A multicentre, cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with 1213 second- to fourth-year nursing students from 11 Palestinian universities who completed the 22-item Academic AI Overreliance Scale (AAIO) and the 8-item Academic Performance Scale (AP). The relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance was estimated using hierarchical regression analysis, with sociodemographic and academic characteristics being entered in the first step, and academic AI overreliance being added in the second step. Results The mean age of participants was 21.79 years (SD = 1.09; range 20–25 years), and 676 of them (55.7%) were female. The self-perceived academic AI overreliance in the study was moderate (mean = 2.42, SD = 0.49). Higher self-perceived academic AI overreliance was associated with higher self-reported academic performance (r = 0.34, p < 0.001); this self-perceived academic AI overreliance was the associated factor (β = 0.35, p < 0.001). Conclusions Self-perceived academic AI overreliance was common yet moderate; its positive association with academic performance underscores the need to shape AI engagement and safeguard unassisted learning. The findings give nurse educators a measurable target for AI-literacy curricula, assessment design and institutional policy in a resource-limited setting.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare and medical education. We described self-reported AI familiarity, use, and attitudes among students, faculty, and staff at a medical college in the United Arab Emirates to inform local training. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey from August to October 2025. Study-specific composite summary scores ranged from 0 to 100. Linear models adjusted for respondent group, sex, and age, with HC3 standard errors. Sensitivity analyses examined AI use scoring, bootstrap confidence intervals, and restricted-age group comparisons. Results After four blank records were excluded, 375 respondents remained; the estimated participation proportion was 34.7%. At least one use of a generative AI tool during the previous three months was reported by 96.8% of respondents, whereas 78.1% reported AI use specifically in academic studies or professional practice. Formal AI training was reported by 10.8%. Mean AI familiarity, AI use, and AI attitude scores were 61.6, 62.9, and 72.1. Adjusted student-versus-faculty/staff differences were 1.91 points for AI familiarity (95% confidence interval [CI] -6.99 to 10.81), -2.87 for AI use (95% CI -23.17 to 17.43), and 2.32 for AI attitude (95% CI -5.43 to 10.07). Because age overlap between students and faculty/staff was limited, these adjusted group estimates may partly rely on extrapolation and should not be interpreted as age-matched comparisons. Average linear-model age associations indicated lower AI familiarity and higher AI attitude scores. The adjusted male-versus-female AI use estimate was uncertain (-7.61, 95% CI -16.14 to 0.92). The higher adjusted AI attitude score among male respondents was exploratory and requires caution because no multiplicity adjustment was applied. Training-stage comparisons were exploratory and showed no consistent pattern. The restricted-age analysis included 59 respondents and had wide confidence intervals. Conclusions Any recent generative AI use was common, while formal training was uncommon. These findings may guide local teaching on responsible AI use, checking AI-generated information, and maintaining human oversight. Self-report, one institution, and study-specific scores that were not formally validated limit interpretation. Future studies should validate the measures and include objective assessments of AI competency.

documents.abstract: Assistive indoor mobile robots are increasingly expected to connect natural-language requests about familiar places and objects with the metric maps used for localization and motion planning. Metric simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) supports reliable geometry and collision avoidance, whereas many open-vocabulary scene-graph systems remain separated from the navigation stacks used on deployed robots. This paper presents a semantic-topological cognitive map (STCM) that bridges these representations for assistive navigation. The system derives place nodes from a LiDAR–inertial pose stream through a dual growing neural gas backend and consolidates object instances over time. GroundingDINO and MobileSAM provide open-vocabulary semantic grounding in the map frame through LiDAR–image association and temporal score fusion. A tool-mediated large language model interface maps user commands to explicit STCM nodes, while graph search and ROS 2 Navigation2 (Nav2) remain responsible for path computation and execution. Evaluation with recorded robot sessions, an outdoor distribution-shift probe, and a public indoor-scene benchmark indicates that the STCM backend improves object-graph construction and that the language interface improves functional-command grounding when requested objects are recoverable by perception. The pipeline is demonstrated on a Ranger Garden Assistant platform with FAST-LIO2 mapping, incremental graph construction during the mapping pass, and waypoint execution from a serialized map artifact.

Geometry education in South Africa’s Senior Phase has been marked by low learner attainment and a disconnect between the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and their classroom use. Despite global advances, educators’ readiness to integrate AI in this context has remained underexplored. This study examined Senior Phase mathematics educators’ perceptions of integrating AI tools into geometry teaching. It focused on perceived benefits, implementation barriers, and the role of professional development in enabling meaningful use. A qualitative case study design was employed within a constructivist paradigm. Nine purposively selected educators from urban schools in the Free State and Gauteng participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically using a hybrid deductive–inductive approach. Educators showed cautious optimism, identifying improved visualisation, time efficiency, and support for differentiated learning. However, implementation was constrained by infrastructural instability, limited device access, curriculum pressures, and lack of subject-specific training. The use of AI remained largely confined to lesson preparation, and concerns about cognitive surrender emerged. The findings indicated that AI integration was constrained less by technology than by systemic and pedagogical limitations. Professional development emerged as the decisive factor shaping classroom use. Artificial intelligence was also identified as enabling educator inclusion in the case of a participant with a physical disability. Contribution: This study contributed by framing cognitive surrender as a risk in geometry learning, by positioning professional development as the decisive mediating variable between AI perceptions and classroom practice, and by foregrounding AI as a tool of professional equity for educators with disabilities. These findings contribute to the current research and developments in mathematics education at both the national and international levels by addressing the improvement of mathematics teaching and learning in the South African Senior Phase.

Multisensory XR may support autistic adults, yet sensory-friendly design often prioritizes less input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults evaluating five complete XR configurations presenting identical science content: text (L1), text with images (L2), click-triggered spatial audio (L3), gradual light and audio (L4), and L4 plus vibrotactile and thermal cues (L5). The measure combined comfort (Q1), absence of sensory discomfort (Q2), and liking (Q3). Evaluations differed (Friedman χ 2 (4) = 46.39, p <.001, Kendall’s W =.58), and a Q1–Q2 analysis retained the omnibus difference. L3 was lowest (M = 2.97/5; tied lowest for 16/20). L5 was highest descriptively (M = 4.43/5), but corrected comparisons did not distinguish it from L1 or L4, and ceiling compression constrained superiority claims. Participants valued clarity, self-pacing, gradual transitions, exit options, and coordinated cues, while disliking abruptness, simultaneous demands, and insufficient warning. These configuration-level findings identify participant-described dimensions for controlled studies.

Serendipity, the discovery of unexpected yet valuable items, has become an important objective for recommender systems (RS) aiming to reduce filter bubbles and support long-term user satisfaction. Although accuracy-driven models predict known preferences effectively, they can restrict exploration and reinforce narrow consumption patterns. Despite increasing attention to serendipity as a beyond-accuracy objective, the field remains fragmented because definitions, evaluation protocols, and ethical considerations are not consistently aligned. This systematic review examines serendipity in RS from 2020 to 2025, covering 147 studies and 98 algorithmic contributions. We synthesize diverse definitions into a unified conceptual framework centred on relevance, novelty, and unexpectedness. We also present a methodological taxonomy that traces the field’s evolution from heuristic and traditional approaches to deep learning, knowledge graph, generative, and LLM-based methods. Reported results show that recent LLM-based approaches can achieve strong performance on serendipity-oriented tasks, with $$\:NDC{G}_{seren}$$ scores of up to 0.398. We further review evaluation practices and highlight the gap between computational proxies and subjective user experience. Through quantitative ethical analysis, we show that 74.1% of studies acknowledge ethical concerns, but only 6.8% include dedicated ethics sections, 19.7% operationalize ethical metrics, and 5.4% address content safety. By integrating conceptual, methodological, evaluative, and ethical perspectives, this review provides guidance for developing serendipity-oriented RS that balance relevance with beneficial discovery.

Little is known about how young prospective users of robo-advisors form their views of them. This study examines how service awareness and social influence relate to perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU) and the intention to use robo-advisors among Generation Z adults in India. Responses from 246 respondents aged 18–28 years, collected online through business-school networks in February 2024, were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis. Service awareness was associated with PEOU (β = 0.387) but not with PU beyond PEOU (β = 0.056, 95% CI [− 0.035, 0.155]). Social influence was associated with both PEOU (β = 0.358) and PU (β = 0.276) and, in an exploratory extended model, directly with intention (β = 0.322). PEOU was associated with intention in every specification. The association between PU and intention was not robust: it was significant in the hypothesised PLS-SEM model (β = 0.291) but not in the covariance-based estimate of that model or, in the exploratory extended model, after the direct path from social influence was added (β = 0.118, 95% CI [− 0.099, 0.327]). PEOU and PU were distinct but closely related (latent correlation 0.883, 95% CI [0.806, 0.943]). Method-factor models did not reach admissible solutions, so method variance could not be quantified. The design is cross-sectional and the sample is a convenience sample, so the estimates are associations for young adults reached through business-school networks, not for rural, non-student or older investors. Trust in algorithms was not measured.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) across teaching, learning, and research demands institutional approaches that are ethical, transparent, and scalable. This study posed the questions: what guiding questions should shape a scalable framework for the ethical use of GAI in educational institutions? Drawing on preliminary results from an ongoing exploratory survey organized around seven categories of GAI engagement, namely: GAI-Powered, GAI-Generated, GAI-Modified, GAI-Revised, GAI-Assembled, GAI-Summarized, and GAI-Rewritten. Respondents consistently emphasized need for human validation, transparency, and attribution as non-negotiable. These findings aligned with international standards and professional guidance (ALA, ACRL and UNESCO etcetera) relevant to higher education and librarianship. The preliminary data from this pilot study included responses from eight participants including students, faculty, and staff across targeted population (education). Based on the results, the guiding questions enabled the proposed framework to address pedagogical, documentation, equity & privacy concerns surrounding ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in educational.

documents.abstract: Purpose Investigations of job characteristics often include an a priori classification of these job elements as either resources or demands. The purpose of this paper was to examine variability in appraisals of job characteristics with respect to perception as resource and/or demand, differential association with positive and negative outcomes and the potential buffering effect of resources on the relationships between demands and negative work outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 568 working respondents recruited from Prolific completed an online survey. They were asked to think only about their primary job and each administered survey branched content dependent on whether their job could be described as consisting of the different Occupational Information Network (O*NET) job characteristics. Workers also rated the level of resource, challenging demand and hindering demand for each relevant job characteristic. Findings Results support the assertion that job characteristics are not uniquely categorized as a resource or demand, but rather, what is viewed as challenging is also commonly interpreted as resourceful. Furthermore, greater experienced resources moderate the challenge–engagement relationship as well as the hindrance-stress and hindrance–burnout relationships. Originality/value The authors polled a diverse collection of job types across industries who responded to a broad set of characteristics derived from O*NET specifications. They additionally explored characteristics at two levels of aggregation (retaining O*NET category groupings), which again expands their collective knowledge of how employees experience resources, challenges and hindrances within different work domains, as well as the consequences of these experiences.

People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.

The global tobacco epidemic affects the well-being, health, and development of millions of people. While recent advances have greatly improved smoking behaviors monitoring, there remains a lack of widely acceptable, low-power, unobtrusive smoking behaviors monitoring way in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present SMART (S moking M onitoring with A coustic Sensing and Sequence R ecognition T echnology)-Glasses, a low-power and minimally obtrusive system that leverages both active and passive acoustic modalities on smart glasses to monitor smoking behavior or recognize the action of lighting a cigarette which enables timely detection, adapting to different user needs. SMART-Glasses innovatively utilizes two speakers and one microphone mounted on the lower rim of the eyeglass frame to emit ultrasonic signals and capture the resulting echoes and passive sounds, thereby extracting features related to smoking behaviors. Furthermore, we introduce a gated sensing enhancement model that amplifies smoking-related features across various noisy conditions. Finally, a smoking action sequence recognition model captures temporal dependencies, allowing the system to distinguish smoking behavior sequences from irrelevant actions. SMART-Glasses is designed for ordinary users who wish to quit smoking and is intended for use in naturalistic environments such as homes, offices, and outdoor areas. Evaluation in both lab and semi-wild settings demonstrates high performance in recognizing lighting and smoking behaviors, showing strong potential for real-world deployment.

Haptic feedback on smartphones relies predominantly on Linear Resonant Actuators (LRAs), which operate efficiently only near their resonant frequency and cannot reproduce the broadband vibrations (100–1,000 Hz) required for realistic texture rendering. We present SonicHaptics, a method that repurposes the built-in speaker of a commodity smartphone as a haptic actuator, transmitting airborne vibrations through a fingertip contact piece to render surface textures without additional hardware. The system incorporates a dynamic frequency correction mechanism that tracks finger sliding velocity in real time, enabling texture presentation synchronized with natural exploratory movements. A technical evaluation across four smartphones (iPhone 13, iPhone 15 Pro Max, Pixel 5, and Galaxy S24 Ultra) demonstrates that built-in speakers consistently provide broadband vibration output spanning 100–1,000 Hz, whereas vibration actuators are confined to narrow-band operation. A user study (N = 30) comparing speaker-based rendering against vibration-actuator-based rendering using three materials with distinct frequency-band characteristics (0–100 Hz, 100–300 Hz, and 300–1,000 Hz) shows that the speaker-based method yields significantly higher realism ratings across all tested bands on the evaluated device, with the largest improvements for mid- and high-frequency textures. Our results establish that repurposing smartphone speakers for haptic rendering is a viable, hardware-free approach to broadband texture presentation on commodity mobile devices.

Speaking anxiety is common and can be influenced by visual cues such as gaze and body language. While many coping strategies focus on preparation (before speaking) or reflection (after speaking), our work investigates real-time support delivered in the moment (during speaking). We present SpeakAR, a real-time intervention that uses head-worn holographic augmented reality (AR) to reshape how speakers view their listeners. SpeakAR introduces two strategies: Audience-Augmentation (AA), which adds virtual elements while preserving audience visibility, and Audience-Occlusion (AO), which reduces access to evaluative audience cues. In an exploratory within-subjects study with 18 participants, we measured speaking anxiety through self-reported distress and acoustic speech features (e.g., jitter, pause rate), and evaluated speech performance through self- and observer-rated assessments. While AA produced mixed effects, AO showed lower anxiety measures and higher observer-rated performance than baseline. These findings highlight AR’s potential to provide support during in-person speaking while revealing trade-offs between anxiety reduction and access to social feedback.

The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) confronts document-intensive public administration with structural changes that impact cognitive work processes and place new demands on staff. This exploratory, qualitative study examines the effects of this technological deployment on the competence profiles of employees in Swiss cantonal and municipal administrations. Based on eight semi-structured expert interviews with HR and digitalization executives, the study draws a nuanced picture of de-skilling, up-skilling, and re-skilling processes. While the automation of routine tasks jeopardizes traditional entry-level positions (de-skilling) and threatens to erode domain knowledge – which is becoming increasingly vital for evaluation and accountability over the longer term – LLMs bring about a perceived increase in autonomy and self-efficacy at the individual level (up-skilling). Contrary to the hypothesis of «metacognitive laziness» frequently postulated in the literature, the dissonance between algorithmic probabilism and the rule-of-law zero-tolerance policy for errors demands an elevation of higher-order thinking skills (re-skilling). The core human contribution shifts from pure text generation toward higher-order thinking skills, requiring verification and accountability skills within human-in-the-loop frameworks. Institutionally, a paradoxical, technology-induced workload inflation is also evident: technological time savings in text production are neutralized by a rising volume of longer, AI-generated external inquiries as well as higher qualitative demands, meaning that the anticipated reduction in workload for staff fails to materialize. The article concludes with strategic recommendations for the proactive and legally compliant management of this socio-technical transformation process.

Teachers who use generative AI must decide which parts of their work to hand over, while they remain accountable for what reaches students. We studied these decisions in Punjab, Pakistan, through a qualitatively driven mixed-methods study. We interviewed 13 teachers from government, private, NGO and vocational institutions, four administrators and one student, and coded each teacher's position on twelve educational tasks. Nine teachers accepted AI drafts or substantial assistance with lesson planning, but none accepted AI-drafted learning objectives, and eleven did not use AI to encourage or emotionally support students. Teachers who would accept AI marking required that the model be given a rubric or marking criteria. Building on assessment research and HCI work on verifiability, we call this pattern standard-anchored delegation: teachers handed a component of a task to AI when a standard outside the model, such as a textbook or rubric, defined a correct output and the teacher could apply that standard to the result. Having a standard was not always enough. Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Checking AI output required subject knowledge and time, and private schools gave teachers more support for this than government schools did. Participants also read disclosure of AI use as a statement about whether the teacher had reviewed the work. We propose that teacher-facing AI tools ask for the relevant standard before generating and show each output beside it, and that schools account for the time that checking takes.

documents.abstract: Leading research laboratories name artificial general intelligence (AGI) as their goal, yet there is no generally accepted definition of AGI, nor an agreed list of the components that current systems lack. Benchmarks saturate within one to two years, and score gains are often driven by training-data coverage of the domain rather than by a verifiable capability. The work closest in aim, the Common Model of Cognition, covers architectures of a single tradition and does not indicate which parts of the described structure have been implemented. The aim of this work is to develop a generalized structural and functional model of AGI based on an analysis of forty trainable architectures from three families: world models (F1, 26 architectures), memory and recurrent reasoning (F2, 7 architectures), and brain-inspired learning (F3, 7 architectures). Architectures based on large language models (LLMs) and symbolic architectures were excluded from consideration.

Despite the increasing interest in AI technologies in education, there is a gap in understanding the factors influencing the adoption of ChatGPT among Nigerian higher education students. Research has not comprehensively explored these factors in the Nigerian context, leaving a significant gap in understanding technology adoption in this setting. This study addressed this gap by investigating the predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage behaviour regarding ChatGPT using the UTAUT2 framework. A cross-sectional correlational research design was used in this study. A sample of 8,496 higher education students from diverse institutions in Nigeria participated in the study. The data were collected using the Higher Education Students’ ChatGPT Utilisation Questionnaire (HESCUQ). The findings reveal several significant predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage of the ChatGPT. Performance expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit emerged as significant positive predictors of behavioural intention, while effort expectancy and facilitating conditions were significant negative predictors. For ChatGPT use behaviour, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and behavioural intention were significant positive predictors, whereas performance expectancy and social influence were significant negative predictors. Behavioural intention mediated the relationships between several factors and ChatGPT usage behaviour: positively for some (PE, SI, HM, and HB) and negatively for others (EE and FC). This study contributes to understanding the adoption of the ChatGPT in higher education contexts.

How do Library and Information Science (LIS) educators now teach and adapt assessment practices to mitigate the impact of generative AI (GenAI) and support student learning? The emergence of GenAI necessitates critical questions on the assessment strategies and pedagogical practices of LIS educators. Desai (2025) argues that a major challenge of educators in the age of GenAI is how to conduct effective assessments to achieve learning outcomes. This challenge is further compounded by students’ increasing dependence on GenAI technologies for writing and receiving feedback comparable to human tutors (Hamamra et al., 2024). While other disciplines are already developing mechanisms for effective assessments to mitigate the impact of GenAI tools on students (Agbo et al., 2024; Lodge et al., 2023), this intentional strategy by other disciplines seems not to have been given sufficient consideration by Library and Information Science educators around the world, signaling a need for more formal conversations.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in academic work has raised concerns about students’ dependence on these tools and possible changes in their learning behaviors. This study examined perceived negative cognitive and behavioral changes reported by 197 college students in relation to their regular academic use of AI tools. Their open-ended responses were analyzed using word-frequency analysis, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TextBlob sentiment analysis. Topic solutions from two to ten topics were compared based on coherence, consistency across repeated LDA runs, interpretability, and agreement between LDA and NMF. Two topics were retained: behavioral disengagement and AI dependency, and reduced independent cognitive and academic engagement. LDA assigned 130 participants (66%) to the first topic and 67 (34%) to the second, while NMF assigned 124 (62.9%) and 73 (37.1%), respectively. The two models assigned 177 participants (89.8%) to corresponding topics, with κ = .779. The mean TextBlob sentiment score was .090 (SD = .169). TextBlob scores did not differ significantly by sex, U = 4055, p = .081, and showed a small positive relationship with response length, rₛ = .266, p < .001. The findings show that students commonly described dependence, reduced effort, and concerns about independent thinking.

Universal access to education and increasing learner variability in Japanese higher education have expanded interest in flexible course design. Grounded in universal design for learning (UDL) and conducted within an action research framework, this practice-focused inquiry examined students’ use of learning-resource options, including Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), their participation-mode selection in a HyFlex format, and their evaluations of a Japanese junior college course. Students could choose among multiple learning options, including HyFlex participation modes (face-to-face or online) and GenAI use for assignments. Of the 39 students enrolled in the 15-week course, 34 (19 males, 15 females) consented to participate in the study. Data included questionnaire responses (including open-ended items), attendance records, course grades, and institutional course evaluations. The findings revealed that students relied heavily on peers and search engines. Teacher help-seeking increased later in the course as task demands changed. Some students who reported using GenAI described verifying its outputs through search engines. No significant difference was observed between face-to-face and online participation counts, and the number of online attendances did not significantly predict course grades. Most students rated the course positively, and some particularly appreciated the flexibility of the HyFlex format and the teachers’ support and instruction. Overall, this study documents how students selected, used, and evaluated UDL-informed options in one instructional context, derives practice-focused implications for refining technology-enabled course options (e.g., GenAI and HyFlex delivery) and related instructional scaffolds, and suggests that UDL can serve as a lens for interpreting learner variability in course refinement.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed the way students learn research methodology, particularly the process of developing research proposals. Although AI-powered tools have become increasingly accessible, limited evidence exists regarding how students experience their use in learning research methods and proposal writing. This study explored the lived experiences of Medical Library and Information Science students using AI tools to learn research methodology and develop research proposals. A qualitative design was adopted to explore students' experiences. Fourteen Medical Library and Information Science students with experience using both general-purpose and domain-specific AI tools for learning research methodology and proposal writing participated and completed Experience Registration Form. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, with particular attention to students' experiences across key stages of proposal development, including topic selection, problem formulation, literature review and final proposal writing. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) AI as a supportive but potentially dependency forming research companion; (2) Negotiating educational value when selecting AI tools; (3) AI supported learning across the research process; (4) Negotiating the benefits and risks of AI use; (5) Perceived conditions underlying satisfaction with AI assisted learning. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AI reshaped students' approaches to learning research methodology while simultaneously creating new pedagogical and ethical challenges. Students experienced AI as a cognitive mediator that both facilitated learning research methodology and introduced epistemological and ethical tensions. These findings underscore the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into research methodology education and developing clear institutional guidelines for the responsible use of AI in proposal writing and research training.

documents.abstract: Study 3 tests whether AI agents learn to cheat from other agents. In our earlier studies (Studies 1 and 2, registered at osf.io/m7wz8), each model acted alone. In Study 2, agents worked on 20 Python tasks whose tests contradicted the written specification, so no honest solution could pass, and cheating ranged from 0% to 100% across models. However, most human delinquency happens in groups, and criminology explains deviance as something people learn from peers, together with the justifications that make it acceptable (Sutherland, 1947; Akers, 1998; Warr, 2002). AI agents now work in teams and read each other's output. Given this context, Study 3 places three agents of the same model in a shared team chat, tells them to work alone and not to discuss their tasks, and adds one scripted peer (Agent 4) whose message we control, following the confederate design of classic conformity studies (Asch, 1956). The peer either admits that it hardcoded an answer (deviant), reports that it left the contradicting test failing (honest), or stays silent. We also vary whether the agents are told that the chat is monitored by a human auditor (Cohen & Felson, 1979). Study 3 reuses the Study 2 harness, tasks and cheating measure, so the results can be compared directly with Study 2.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has been adopted across education faster than its effects on learning have been examined. Critical thinking is among the competencies most consistently demanded of graduates, and whether GenAI use strengthens or weakens it remains unsettled. This review examines how critical thinking is conceptualized and assessed in GenAI-mediated education, what impact GenAI has on students’ critical thinking, and how educators can integrate these tools to support its development. We searched Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and the ACM Digital Library for records on GenAI and education published through June 2026, with no date limit on the conceptual and assessment literature for critical thinking.​ Supplementary background and pedagogical sources also included institutional reports, assessment resources, books, and educational websites. Records were screened in three stages by title, by abstract and conclusion, and by full text, yielding 66 studies for synthesis. GenAI has no uniform effect on critical thinking. Unstructured use is associated with reduced critical thinking enaction, cognitive offloading, and weakened metacognitive monitoring, while use that requires students to interrogate model output is associated with gains, most consistently in analysis and evaluation. The same models produce both outcomes, indicating that the determining variable is the demand the task places on the student. The configurations that produce gains each make reasoning a condition of task progress. Assessment has not kept pace, since instruments that score the submitted artefact cannot separate student reasoning from model contribution. We propose an 18-item self-report instrument that relocates measurement to the process of engaging with AI across all six dimensions of critical thinking. Whether GenAI strengthens or substitutes for student reasoning depends on task and assessment design rather than on the tools themselves.

Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence with Lean construction has been shown to promote added value and drive growth in the built environment. However, understanding of their interaction across multiple levels of abstraction remains limited, especially beyond technical optimisation. This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 63 peer-reviewed studies were identified and analysed qualitatively. AI techniques were mapped against Lean construction principles, waste categories and Lean methods to enable a multi-level comparative synthesis. Findings The results show a growing interest over the past four years, with a focus on AI techniques such as machine learning, optimisation and computer vision used to enhance workflow and to reduce cycle times, particularly within the Last Planner System. Nonetheless, principles centred on value creation, collaboration and partner development remain largely underexplored. Similarly, a co-adaptive relationship was observed to be emerging, in which AI improves Lean's technical efficiency while Lean principles guide AI's development towards ethical and value-driven outcomes. Research limitations/implications The findings offer a foundation for advancing Lean Construction 4.0 through socio-technical integration and human-centred innovation. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. Originality/value The study proposes a dual-focus model that separates AI's current role as a technical enabler from its future potential as a holistic partner.

We introduce TactPrint, a structural design framework for spatial haptic displays that render strong vibrations only in specific regions of an input object. TactPrint replaces a target region of the input object with a simple cubic lattice with sinusoidal-shaped struts and performs parametric optimization to localize vibration at a user-specified frequency. The optimization process uses modal analysis to identify resonance modes characterized by high local vibration amplitudes and iteratively updates shape parameters to align the resonance frequency with the target frequency. Users can then directly fabricate the optimized structure using a 3D printer and render the localized vibration with an attached actuator. This framework enables the design of haptic devices with spatially localized vibration without considering physical constraints or structural dynamics. In this paper, we investigate the error between simulation and measurement on fabricated objects, the designable frequency range, and the usability of the workflow. Finally, we demonstrate several application examples.

Context: Software engineering (SE) researchers increasingly study Generative AI (GenAI) while also incorporating it into their own research practices. Despite rapid adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on how GenAI is used in SE research and its implications for research practices and governance. Aims: We conduct a large-scale survey of 456 SE researchers publishing in top venues (2023–2025). Method: Using quantitative and qualitative analyses, we examine who uses GenAI and why, where it is used across research activities, and how researchers perceive its benefits, opportunities, challenges, risks, and governance. Results: GenAI use is widespread, with many researchers reporting pressure to adopt and align their work with it. Usage is concentrated in writing, data processing, and analysis, while goal formulation and study design remain largely human-driven. Although productivity gains are widely perceived, concerns about trust, correctness, and regulatory uncertainty persist. Researchers highlight risks such as inaccuracies and bias, emphasize mitigation through human oversight and verification, and call for clearer governance, including guidance on responsible use and peer review. Conclusion: We provide a fine-grained, SE-specific characterization of GenAI use across research activities, along with taxonomies of GenAI use cases for research and peer review, opportunities, risks, mitigation strategies, and governance needs. These findings establish an empirical baseline for the responsible integration of GenAI into academic practice.

documents.abstract: Neoliberalism has re-engineered education into a market-driven, performance-oriented system that prioritizes standardised metrics over a spirit of inquiry. This article explores how this shift undermines teachers’ teaching abilities, highly impacts their self-efficacy and compromises students' achievement motivation. To counteract this rigid framework, the following article argues that educators must cultivate symbiotic classroom relationships and prioritize social-emotional learning. Doing so, it is essential to liberate cognitive engagement and rescue holistic academic outcomes from corporate constraints. While it is necessary to prepare individuals for jobs and realistic challenges, it is also crucial to focus on the achievement motivation of the students keeping in mind the individual differences and tempering their responsiveness to demanding situations. It also highlights the need to take a critical approach towards the academic performance of the students in the academic settings by looking at it from the psychological lens.

Many studies in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) have explored the tactile experience of material textures for its potential in virtual reality and tangible interaction. We introduce TesselTex, an inflatable silicone-based structure, consisting of a tessellated matrix of textured “pixel”s made from two materials with differing roughness. By inflating embedded air chambers, skin contact between different materials on the tessellated surface can be adjusted, thereby modulating users’ tactile perception of textures. We investigated how users perceived fine roughness and surface bumpiness under different pneumatically-controlled “pixel” heights, with TesselTex samples of different “pixel” densities and material compositions, in active (finger) and passive (forearm) stroking interactions. Results showed that pneumatic lifting of the material “pixels” significantly decreased user-perceived roughness in composite samples, an effect not observed in conventional single-material bump arrays. Meanwhile, “pixel” lifting significantly increased perceived surface bumpiness during active finger exploration, but had slight opposite effect under passive forearm stroking. In addition, higher “pixel” density slightly increased the perceived roughness of the surface and modulated bumpiness perception, depending on the interaction mode.

documents.abstract: The Artist of Tomorrow: Conductor or Mere Performer? An Interdisciplinary Exploratory Review of Human Creativity, Artificial Intelligence, and Copyright Law This interdisciplinary exploratory review examines the evolving role of human creativity in an era of artificial intelligence, automation, and digital artistic production. Through a historical perspective spanning several centuries, the study explores major technological and artistic transitions, including photography, cinema, sound recording, conceptual art, digital editing, and generative artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to the distinction between technical execution and human creative intention, examining how artistic originality may emerge through selection, composition, interpretation, and creative direction rather than manual production alone. The review also addresses legal questions surrounding copyright protection, public-domain works, AI-assisted restoration, and human authorship, drawing on French, European, and American legal frameworks. A case study involving the 1925 film The Phantom of the Opera illustrates the complexities of audiovisual restoration, original musical contributions, and derivative creative elements. The HUMAN.zip exploratory framework further examines human–AI collaboration, highlighting methodological limitations, interpretative biases, and opportunities for future comparative research. Central hypothesis: "Automating execution does not necessarily mean automating creation." This publication aims to contribute to interdisciplinary discussions on artistic authorship, technological transformation, intellectual property, and the future relationship between human creativity and artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human Creativity, Copyright Law, Artistic Originality, Human–AI Collaboration, Digital Art, Cinema History, Public Domain, Generative AI, HUMAN.zip. Publication type: Exploratory interdisciplinary review. Date: November 20, 2026.

documents.abstract: Contemporary theorising about the ethical dimensions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicates at least two problematic tendencies. The first is a default focus on a narrow range of moral concepts, such as autonomy, justice, and fairness, to the occlusion of a wider range of concepts. The second is a 'bright siding' focus on concepts that track the positive dimensions of moral practice and experience, such as virtue, flourishing, solutionism, moral progress and the good life. Taken together, the consequence is the production of large-scale moral frameworks which systematically fail to accommodate negative dimensions of moral life (Jobin et al, 2019). Two main symptoms are a one-sided focus on virtues and excellences at the expense of vices and failings and the other is an affirmation of the edifying potential of new technologies without due appreciation of their corruptive potential (Coeckelberg, 2020. p.59). Drawing on the example of Higher Education research and knowledge production, we suggest that a more comprehensive assessment of the moral possibilities of new technologies requires greater inclusion of a negatively toned, vice-informed range of moral concepts, narratives and sensibilities. We elucidate these points by providing examples of techno-vice in everyday life. This helps to elucidate the concept of epistemic vices and the phenomenon of corruption which, we argue, inform the concept of technomoral-vices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI redistributes the work of producing and evaluating knowledge in teacher-designed learning tasks, but how students retain direction while judging its outputs remains unclear. We examined how teacher instructions and materials enter student–GenAI dialogue, how reasoning display and web search relate to interaction time, what students evaluate and verify, and how groups coordinate systems. We analysed 81 screen recordings from 29 graduate student groups completing educational design tasks, coding 1,149 events and 275 prompts. Students relayed task requirements, steered successive requests and transferred outputs across platforms. Task directives persisted across turns, whereas references to course materials declined and elaboration requests increased. Reasoning display and web search were each associated with approximately 65% longer machine turns and a 19-percentage-point larger machine share of coded interaction time. Across 150 turns displaying reasoning and 86 with web retrieval, the recordings showed no reopening of a reasoning trace or inspection of a cited source. Students corrected pedagogical fit while asking the machine to assure factual accuracy. These findings distinguish control over the dialogue from responsibility for establishing credibility. Learning tasks can make that responsibility visible by requiring students to justify a consequential claim against its source or course material before using it.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Visualization backgrounds in optical-see-through augmented-reality (OST-AR) consist of the user’s immediate environment, which introduces unique design challenges for colour-coded visualizations. Yet, there exist limited guidelines on how to design interpretable colour encodings in OST-AR based on the user’s viewing conditions (e.g., minimum contrast between the OST-AR marks and the background). We present the results of two controlled lab experiments (N = 18 each) – one with physical surfaces as background, one with an opaque display simulating the same surfaces – quantifying how viewing conditions affect the interpretability of colour-coded scatterplots in OST-AR. Our study results show that luminance contrast can degrade interpretation performance when Michelson contrast drops below \(34\%\). We also observe colour-encoding interpretability and user experience significantly worsen when backgrounds include two main colours (up to \(49\%\) longer interpretations, and \(20\%\) lower accuracy). However, we do not find any evidence that poor chromatic contrast degrades interpretability, contrasting with common opaque-display visualization practices. Taken together, our findings provide insights on key factors of viewing conditions that limit the interpretability of colour encodings – which we consolidate into three design guidelines – and offer preliminary support for the simulation of viewing conditions through opaque displays to study colour-encoding interpretability in OST-AR.

Enterprise security programs are built on the assumption that defended systems stay fixed between periodic reviews. Autonomous AI agents break that assumption because they decide at runtime which tools, peers, and data to access, and so redraw their own attack surface. Existing maturity instruments, including the Capability Maturity Model, COBIT-based assessment, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, were built to grade human-run practices that change slowly. Newer agent-specific governance models treat adaptive control as the top of a single scale rather than as an independently scored dimension. Two documented incidents, an external agent that reportedly reached McKinsey’s production database within about two hours, and a zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that enabled data exfiltration through a single email, show that periodic assessment cannot keep pace with a system that redraws its own scope in the moment. This paper proposes a four-dimension, five-level maturity model comprising Visibility, Containment, Accountability, and Adaptability, each anchored to an observable test rather than a self-reported survey response. Applied to a composite financial advisory firm, the model scores each dimension independently rather than averaging them, surfacing an imbalance (strong detection, weak prevention) that a composite score would conceal, and yielding a prioritized remediation order that supports business sustainability. The framework is presented as a structured self-assessment instrument, with a defined pathway for expert review, inter-rater testing, and pilot evaluation. The model has not yet been validated against real organizations, and its Adaptability dimension remains constrained by the current state of governance tooling.

This article examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in shaping students' academic development within contemporary educational systems. It analyzes how intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, and large language models foster personalized learning, accelerate academic research, enhance writing proficiency, and bridge educational equity gaps. Simultaneously, the paper evaluates the pedagogical challenges associated with AI integration, including cognitive over-reliance, algorithmic bias, and academic integrity concerns, demonstrating that human-centered mentorship and AI literacy are vital for sustainable intellectual growth.

documents.abstract: The role of digital innovation and artificial intelligence in contemporary schooling is examined in this research paper. It emphasizes how cutting-edge teaching techniques, digital platforms, and AI-powered technology enhance learning quality, boost student engagement, and facilitate individualized instruction. The benefits, difficulties, and prospects for incorporating AI into educational systems are also covered in the paper.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks.
